No source here proves that anyone classically said David conquered Jerusalem absolutely alone in the historical sense.

paragraphs.text: The supported origin of the idea is not that David had no help at all, but that the Tanakh explicitly credits him with the capture of the stronghold: “David captured the stronghold of Zion” and “David occupied the stronghold.”. That wording can easily become homiletic language that Jerusalem is “David’s possession,” even though the same verses also say that David’s men were with him and that Joab was the first to attack and later rebuild parts of the city.

Abarbanel makes the strongest explicit claim in that direction. He says that the verse means David himself, because of his bravery, captured the fortress first, and that it was therefore called by his name rather than Joab’s. He then uses Chronicles to refine the story: David commanded the capture, Joab went up first, and Joab received the promised rank. So Abarbanel is not saying David had literally no participant around him; he is emphasizing that the city is credited to David.

Chronicles also helps explain where the “single-handed” flavor comes from. It juxtaposes “David and all Israel” going to Jerusalem with the statement that David himself captured the citadel, while separately saying Joab went up first and later “restored” the rest of the city. In other words, the text assigns the conquest to David as king, while acknowledging Joab’s tactical role.

Samuel adds another layer: David speaks as the leader who sets the terms for the assault, promising rank to “whoever attacks the Jebusites first.”. That is the opposite of a claim that nobody else was involved, but it does show that David is the one who frames and owns the victory narrative.

Rabbeinu Bahya shows a later rabbinic move in the same direction: he cites a Midrash on “David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is the City of David,” and takes the name as a theological statement about why Jerusalem bears David’s name. That supports a symbolic reading of “David’s possession,” though it still does not say he personally acted entirely alone.

Josephus likewise is not “single-handed” in the literal sense: he says David and the people came to Jerusalem, that David laid siege, and that Joab was the one who first got into the citadel. This is another witness that the classical tradition can credit David with the conquest while still recognizing the participation of others.

So the best-supported answer is: the phrase likely comes from a homiletic reading of “David captured the stronghold” in Samuel and Chronicles, reinforced by Abarbanel and related interpretations that stress David’s ownership of the conquest and the city’s being named for him. It is not supported as a literal historical claim that he acted with no assistance whatsoever.

question_html:
Where did the idea that David conquered Jerusalem "single handedly" come from?

I saw a clip by R' Shlomo Carlebach where he claimed that Jerusalem is "David's possession" because he conquered it single handedly. This seems to go against basic Tanach, as well as Midrash (e.g. the Midrash about him lifting Yoav up on a tree etc.)

Nonetheless, Reb Shlomo knew his stuff so I want to give him the benefit of the doubt - whence this idea?

research_plan.context: The question is in Tanakh/midrash/history, not practical halacha. The likely issue is whether any classic source says David took Jerusalem alone or uniquely, and whether Reb Shlomo Carlebach was paraphrasing a textual idea rather than asserting literal military history. A possible premise error is that the phrase may reflect a homiletic reading of "וילכד דוד את מצודת ציון" or a midrashic contrast between David and Yoav, not a claim that no one else assisted.

Do any midrashim or commentaries describe David as acting alone, or only emphasize his leadership and merit?
Is Carlebach likely paraphrasing a verse, midrash, or later homiletic tradition about David’s possession of Jerusalem?
Does any source connect David’s conquest of Jerusalem with a legal or symbolic notion of ownership rather than a literal battlefield claim?

en: David and all Israel set out for Jerusalem, that is Jebus, where the Jebusite inhabitants of the land lived. David was told by the inhabitants of Jebus, “You will never get in here!” But David captured the stronghold of Zion; it is now the City of David. David said, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites first will be the chief officer”; Joab son of Zeruiah attacked first, and became the chief. David occupied the stronghold; therefore it was renamed the City of David. David also fortified the surrounding area, from the Millo round about, and Joab rebuilt the rest of the city. David kept growing stronger, for GOD of Hosts was with him.
sources.title: I Chronicles 11:4-9

en: The king and his men set out for Jerusalem against the Jebusites who inhabited the region. David was told, “You will never get in here! Even the blind and the lame will turn you back.” (They meant: David will never enter here.) c Even the blind … enter here Meaning of Heb. uncertain. sources.text: he: והבן הפסוקים שראשונה אמר וילכד דוד את מצודת ציון היא עיר דוד, ר"ל שהם היו נלחמים עם העיר ועם המבצר ודוד בעצמו לגבורתו ראשונה לכד המבצר, ולכבודו וכבוד המבצר ההוא קראו עיר דוד ולא נקרא עוד מצודה, ולא לכד יואב המצודה ההיא כי אם דוד עצמו, ולכן נקראה על שמו, ואחרי שלכד דוד המצודה השתדל ללכוד עוד את העיר שהיתה גם כן חזקה מאד והיתה נבדלת מהמבצר, (ח) וז"ש אח"כ כל מכה יבוסי ויגע בצנור ואת העורים והפסחים שנאי נפש דוד, ר"ל שצוה דוד על לכידת העיר ואמר שכל אשר יכה ראשונה היבוסי, והוא שיכנס ראשונה בעיר ויגע בצנור שהוא המגדל החזק שאשר יגע בו ראשונה ויגיע עדיו, ועם זה יכה כלם אפילו העורים והפסחים. ואמרו שנאי נפש דוד לא יחזור לבד לעורים ולפסחים כי אם לכל הנזכרים, והם היבוסי והעורים והפסחים שהיו שונאים אותו ואומרים לבזותו לא תבא הנה. והנה גזרת המאמר לא נזכר בכאן, ובדברי הימים אמר (דברי הימים א' י"א ה' ו') ויאמרו יושבי יבוס לדוד לא תבא הנה וילכוד דוד את מצודת ציון היא עיר דוד, ויאמר דוד כל מכה יבוסי בראשונה יהיה לראש ולשר ויעל בראשונה יואב בן צרויה ויהי לראש: והנה למדנו מזה שנכתב בדברי הימים דברים. אחד שאחרי שלכד דוד מצודת ציון צוה על הכות יבוסי והיא לכידת העיר כמו שאמרתי. השני שגזרת המאמר הוא יהיה לראש ולשר. השלישי שלא אמר שיהיה לראש כל מי שיכה יבוסי, כי אם שהראשון שיכנס ויעלה שמה בחזקה יתנו לו שררה ושלטנות. הרביעי שיואב הוא היה אשר עלה ראשונה והדברים האלה כלם לא נזכרו בכאן. החמישי שלא זכר שם עורים ופסחים, והוא מה שיורה שלא היו מעצם הספור כי אם הרחבת הלשון ודבור המשלי, כמו שזכרתי. ואמרו הנה על כן יאמרו עור ופסח לא יבא אל הבית, הוא משל דבריהם אשר אמרו, והוא דבור בלעג ובתמיהה, כאומר עור ופסח יאמר לדוד לא תבוא הנה, כמו שאמרו היבוסים? זה היה באמת סכלות גדול:

en: I have found a Midrash which supports this. Our sages commented on Samuel II 5,7 where we read וילכוד דוד את מצודת ציון היא עיר דוד, “David captured the citadel of David which became the city of David.” The Midrash asks why the city was called after a mortal, i.e. after King David? The answer provided is that G’d knew perfectly well that the city would initially be built and subsequently destroyed by mortal human beings. This is why during the periods preceding the final Temple, Jerusalem was known as the city of David, i.e. the city of a mortal human being. However, in the future, it will bear the name of G’d Himself seeing that it would then no longer be subject to destruction. This is the meaning of Isaiah 60,14 והלכו אליך שחוח בני מעניך והשתחוו....וקראו לך עיר ה' ציון קדוש ישראל, “they shall come before you, the children of those who have tormented you....and you will be called ‘city of the Lord, Zion, the Holy One of Israel.”

sources.text: … כל שכן שנושא את עצמו (סוטה שם. וראה לעיל). וְלֹא אָבָה דָוִד לְהָסִיר אֵלָיו אֶת אֲרוֹן ה' עַל עִיר דָּוִד - היא ציון (רד"ק) - וַיַּטֵּהוּ דָוִד בֵּית עֹבֵד אֱדוֹם הַגִּתִּי (שמואל שם י), שהיה לוי (במדבר רבה (וילנא) ד כ) מן השוערים (רש"י שמואל שם). הארון היה שם במשך שלשה חדשים (שמואל שם יא), ואז העלהו דוד לעיר דוד (שם יב), היא ציון (מצודת דוד), ושם ישב הארון באהל בְּתוֹךְ הַיְרִיעָה (שם ז ב), עד שבנה שלמה את הבית הראשון והכניסו לקדש הקדשים. גניזת הארון בבית ראשון ארון הקדש - יחד עם צנצנת המן, וצלוחית שמן המשחה, ומקלו של אהרן ושקדיה ופרחיה, וארגז ששגרו פלשתים דורון לאלהי ישראל - נגנז בימי המלך יאשיהו, כשלשים וחמש שנה קודם לחורבן הבית הראשון. ונחלקו תנאים בדבר: יש סוברים שהארון נגנז במקומו, שנאמר (מלכים א ח ח): וַיִּהְיוּ שָׁם עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (רבי יהושע בן לוי בתוספתא סוטה יג א, ובבלי יומא נג ב; רבי שמעון בן יוחאי יומא שם ונד א; רבי שמעון בן לקיש בירושלמי שקלים ו א), או שנגנז בלשכת דיר העצים שבמקדש (שקלים ו א; חכמים ביומא שם, ובירושלמי שם), וכשבנה שלמה את הבית וידע שסופו ליחרב - בנה בו מקום לגנוז בו הארון למטה במטמוניות עמוקות ועקלקלות (רמב"ם בית הבחירה ד א), ויאשיהו המלך גנזו, שנאמר: וַיֹּאמֶר לַלְוִיִּם וגו' תְּנוּ אֶת אֲרוֹן הַקֹּדֶשׁ בַּבַּיִת אֲשֶׁר בָּנָה שְׁלֹמֹה בֶן דָּוִיד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין לָכֶם מַשָּׂא בַּכָּתֵף (דברי הימים ב לה ג), הרי שגנז את הארון (ברייתא יומא נב ב; רבי יהושע בן לוי בתוספתא שם, ובירושלמי שם; רמב"ם בית הבחירה ד א, וראה שקלים ו א). ויש סוברים שגלה לבבל, שנאמר: וַיְבִאֵהוּ בָבֶלָה (דברי הימים ב לו י), ונאמר בנבואת ישעיה לחזקיה: וְנִשָּׂא כָּל אֲשֶׁר בְּבֵיתֶךָ וגו' בָּבֶל לֹא יִוָּתֵר דָּבָר (ישעיה לט ו) - אלו עשרת הדברות שבו (רבי אליעזר ורבי שמעון תוספתא סוטה שם, ובבלי יומא נג ב, וירושלמי שקלים שם). בבית שני בבית שני לא היה הארון לדברי הכל, והוא אחד מחמשה דברים שהיו בין מקדש ראשון למקדש שני (יומא כא ב). ומפני שנגנזו הלוחות לא עשו ארון אחר, שהרי עיקר מצות עשית הארון כדי להניח שם את הלוחות (מנחת חנוך צה; משך חכמה שמות כה כא. ועי' רש"ש ליומא נג ב, ושו"ת חתם סופר יו"ד רלו). על הכפורת והכרובים ראה ערכם. הערות שוליים ב, עמ' קעד2 – קעט1. ↑ וראה קדמוניות ליוסף בן מתתיהו ג ו א, שעשו מעצי שטים כדי שלא יתליעו. וראה רש"י יומא עב א ד"ה שמעמידין. ↑ ולדעת הסוברים, שהיו שמונה טבעות קבועות בארון וארבעה בדים בהן, לא נאסרו רק ארבע מהן שלא יסורו הבדים מתוכן, אבל שני הבדים האחרים לא היו קבועים, שנתנום בטבעות רק בשעת מסע המחנה, ובשעת חנייה היו מסירים אותם (תוספות יומא שם ד"ה כתיב. וראה מלבי"ם שמות שם) ↑ והוא מפרש הכתוב: וְשַׂמְתֶּם אֹתוֹ מִצַּד אֲרוֹן בְּרִית־ה' אֱלֹהֵיכֶם (דברים לא כו) , מצד הוא מונח, ולא בתוכו (בבא בתרא שם) . ↑ על מהותם ראה מלואים לתורה שלמה פר' תרומה, סוף כרך כב. ↑

sources.question_context: Wikipedia says: The city of Jerusalem has been surrounded by walls for its defense since ancient times. In the Middle Bronze Age, a period also known in biblical terms as the era of the Patriarchs, a city named Jebus was built on the southeastern hill of Jerusalem, relatively small (50,000 square meters) but well fortified. Remains of its walls are located above the Siloam Tunnel. From my recollection, the first mention in Tanac"h that Jerusalem had a wall is in Melachim (Kings) I 3:1 where it says that Shlomo built the wall of Jerusalem. However, based on above, it seems that the city had a wall for a long period prior to that. Who built the first wall and when?
sources.relevance_reason: Contains discussion of the Jerusalem wall and cites 1 Chronicles 11:8 with Rashi; useful background on the extent of David's conquest and later rebuilding, though not directly about 'single-handedly'.

Answer 1 (levi cohen): There are many parts to yerushalayim, the part today known as "ir david" was the city of yerushalayim as it was in the times of the yevusim (fortified with walls and towers etc.) and thats what david conquered. shlomo hamelech expanded the walls to include up to and including har hamoriah. the city continued to be expanded by diffrent kings: chizkiyahu, herod, aggripas etc.

sources.question_context: David takes over Jerusalem (finally) in Shmuel II, Perek 5. It says that David wants to be rid of the סירך ועורים. This is commonly translated as the blind and the lame. Metzudat David understands this to actually mean that David needed/wanted to get rid of the handicapped people in Jerusalem in order to take it over. Ralbag understands this to mean that they are two statues at the front of the city that make it hard to get in as they each lift and drop their sticks (powered by the aqueduct) (much like mini-golf of today). What does David really mean when he wants to destroy them? He even offers an award to the one who does it. Is it possible he really does want to destroy the handicapped, and if so how to we assimilate that idea with our idea of David?
sources.relevance_reason: Explains the 'blind and the lame' passage in Samuel 5 and shows how commentators contextualize David's conquest of Jerusalem, which helps interpret the surrounding verses.
sources.text: As you said, Ralbag (and most of the commentaries) understand this to be talking about statues of some kind. (Metzudas David to 5:8 also cites this as a second explanation.) So according to that view of things, David had nothing against the blind and lame people any more than against any of the other Jebusites. Metzudas David's first explanation (to 5:6), though, is indeed that it means people suffering from these handicaps. However, he explains the mention of them as part of the Jebusites' boast: "Our tower [this is his explanation of צנור in that verse] is so strongly fortified that even if its only remaining defenders were the blind and the lame, you would still be unable to conquer it!" So David's challenge to his men (v. 8) is: "Disprove their claim! First topple the tower while it is still defended by all of the Jebusite army, and only then deal with these insolent Jebusites - including the blind and lame people, all of whom had joined in jeering us."
sources.title: What are the "blind and the lame" that David wanted to be rid of when he entered Jerusalem, and what does that mean?

sources.question_context: In the book of Samuel 2, Chapter 6:17 it says: They brought in the Ark of the LORD and set it up in its place inside the tent which David had pitched for it, and David sacrificed burnt offerings and offerings of well-being before the LORD. How long had King David been reigning in Jerusalem prior to this event?
sources.relevance_reason: Gives a timeline showing David conquered Jerusalem after reigning in Hebron, which helps frame the event historically and makes a 'single-handedly' literal reading less plausible.
sources.text: According to Samuel 1:7:2 , the Ark was in Kiryath-jearim for 20 years. According to Seder Olam Rabbah , this period encompasses the ca. 11 years of Shmuel's time as judge, ca. two years of Shaul as king, and ca. 7.5 years of David as king in Hebron. After 7.5 years in Hebron David conquered Jerusalem ( Samuel 2:5:4-9 ), so that means that shortly after that, sometime into his eighth year, he made his first attempt at bringing the Ark. That attempt failed, and the Ark waited another three months before David's second attempt ( Samuel 2:6:11 ; Chronicles 1:13:14 ), which is the one you're asking about. This likely occurred around the end of David's eighth year. So it seems that David ruled in Jerusalem for less than a year or about a year before the Ark was brought there.
sources.title: How long did King David reign in Jerusalem before he brought the Ark there?

evidence.claim: The supported origin of the idea is not that David had no help at all, but that the Tanakh explicitly credits him with the capture of the stronghold: “David captured the stronghold of Zion” and “David occupied the stronghold.”
evidence.quote: But David captured the stronghold of Zion; it is now the City of David.

evidence.claim: That wording can easily become homiletic language that Jerusalem is “David’s possession,” even though the same verses also say that David’s men were with him and that Joab was the first to attack and later rebuild parts of the city.
evidence.quote: The king and his men set out for Jerusalem

support_checks.reason: Supported: Tanakh credits David with the capture while also mentioning Joab and David’s men.

evidence.claim: Abarbanel makes the strongest explicit claim in that direction.
evidence.quote: דוד בעצמו לגבורתו ראשונה לכד המבצר

evidence.claim: He says that the verse means David himself, because of his bravery, captured the fortress first, and that it was therefore called by his name rather than Joab’s.
evidence.quote: ולכבודו וכבוד המבצר ההוא קראו עיר דוד

evidence.claim: He then uses Chronicles to refine the story: David commanded the capture, Joab went up first, and Joab received the promised rank.
evidence.quote: ויעל בראשונה יואב בן צרויה ויהי לראש

evidence.claim: So Abarbanel is not saying David had literally no participant around him; he is emphasizing that the city is credited to David.
evidence.quote: ולא לכד יואב המצודה ההיא כי אם דוד עצמו

support_checks.reason: Supported: Abarbanel explicitly stresses David’s own conquest and distinguishes Joab’s role.
support_checks.verified_text: Abarbanel makes the strongest explicit claim in that direction. evidence.claim: Chronicles also helps explain where the “single-handed” flavor comes from.

evidence.claim: Josephus likewise is not “single-handed” in the literal sense: he says David and the people came to Jerusalem, that David laid siege, and that Joab was the one who first got into the citadel.
This is another witness that the classical tradition can credit David with the conquest while still recognizing the participation of others.
